title: The City of God (after 410)
hook: Rome is sacked, and Augustine writes of two cities built by two loves
tomorrow: Love, and do what you will

segments.voice: Yesterday, late have I loved thee, and God called pulchritudo, a beauty ever ancient, ever new. What old thing did you see as if for the first time? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

News travels across the sea to North Africa: Rome has been sacked by the Goths. Not a border town. Rome. The city that had seemed as permanent as the sky. Refugees arrive with stories. And some of the people who still honor the old gods say out loud what others are whispering: this is what happens when an empire abandons its gods for the Christian one. Augustine, a bishop in a harbor town, hears it. He doesn't answer with a quick sermon. He starts writing, and keeps writing, book after book, until the answer becomes the work he calls The City of God.
screen: `ROME HAS BEEN SACKED.` → `THEY BLAME THE CHRISTIANS.` → `AUGUSTINE STARTS TO WRITE.`

segments.voice: First, the question underneath. If God is on our side, how could Rome fall? Augustine's answer begins by moving the ground. No city on earth was ever God's guarantee. Empires rise and fall. Something else is being built. Second, the heart of it, in book fourteen. Two loves, he says, have made two cities. The earthly city is built by love of self, reaching even to contempt of God. The heavenly city is built by love of God, reaching even to contempt of self. Notice where the line runs: by love, not by address. Rome is not simply the earthly city. And though Augustine can call the Church the city of God, he says that on earth even the Church holds some who will not share its end, while some of its present enemies will. Third, the two are tangled together. In this world, Augustine says, the two cities are mixed together, tangled, until the last judgment. Some readers hear Jesus's parable of the wheat and the weeds in that. You can't draw a map. The same street, the same family, sometimes the same heart, holds both loves pulling against each other. Fourth, how to live in the meantime. Augustine calls the city of God a pilgrim on earth. Pilgrims don't despise the towns they pass through. They use the roads, keep the peace, pray for the place, the way the prophet Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city. But they don't mistake it for home. So the fall of Rome, for Augustine, was terrible and real. It just wasn't the end of the story. For Augustine, the city that mattered most had never had walls.
screen: `NO CITY IS GOD'S GUARANTEE.` · `TWO LOVES MADE TWO CITIES.` · `TANGLED TOGETHER UNTIL THE END.` · `A PILGRIM CITY ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `TWO LOVES, TWO CITIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask which city you're building. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day. Pick three things you did with real effort: a task, a conversation, a decision. For each one, ask Augustine's question gently. Which love was doing the building? Was it mostly about me, my comfort, my image? Or was it turned toward God, or toward someone else's good? Don't grade yourself. A day can hold both. Just notice where the bricks went. If you pray, you can offer tomorrow's work to God before you start it. The bell holds the time.
civitas Dei. Latin for the city of God, Augustine's name for the heavenly city built by love of God, tangled with the earthly one until the end. Today's word.
Your line: two loves, two cities. Today, do one small thing for the peace of the place you live, the way Augustine's pilgrims would. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: When the Second Vatican Council describes the Church in Lumen Gentium 8, it quotes The City of God on the Church pressing forward like a pilgrim, amid the world's persecutions and God's consolations.

fork.setup: Rome has been sacked, and your neighbors blame the Christians. you're Augustine. where do you draw the line between the two cities?
options: between two loves, running through every heart.
fork.reveal: two loves made two cities, he says: love of self and love of God. they're mixed together until the end, so you can't draw them on a map.

original.note: Latin: the city of God — the title Augustine gave his work.

trapdoor: what you thought: the city of God means heaven, or maybe the Vatican.
what it means: two cities built by two loves, tangled together on earth, one of them a pilgrim on the road home.
what a scholar hears: De civitate Dei 14.28 — love of self to contempt of God, love of God to contempt of self — written to answer pagan critics after the sack of Rome.

notes: City of God 14.28 is paraphrased (Dods 1871 is public domain but not on the validator's list); confirm the paraphrase.

The wheat-and-weeds image for the mixed cities: Augustine uses the parable of the tares in several places on the mixed Church; confirm that tying it to the two cities here is fair, or cite 1.35 (intermixed) only.
City of God 19.26 cites Jeremiah 29:7 on seeking the peace of Babylon; confirm reference.
'Pilgrim' (peregrinans) for the city of God on earth: confirm. howItsDone's link to Lumen Gentium's pilgrim Church is a soft echo; confirm wording.
Hook: the sack of Rome and pagan blame of Christians is the occasion Augustine gives in his Retractations and in book 1; no date stated in the voice (the date is in the index title only).
'A bishop in a harbor town' = Hippo; not named to keep it simple.

Editor pass: the wheat-and-weeds image is no longer put in Augustine's mouth ('some readers hear' it); match pair changed to match. Practice wording and carry changed so they don't duplicate day 740's 'check the root' practice and carry; the carry now takes the pilgrim/peace-of-the-city angle.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix. The teach said Augustine 'doesn't say ... the other is the Church'; he does identify the city of God with the Church in places (e.g. City of God 8.24, 'the city of God, which is the holy Church'; also 13.16, 20.9), while also saying the Church on earth is mixed (1.35). Reworded to say the line runs by love, Rome is not simply the earthly city, and the Church on earth holds both. Keeper: confirm 8.24 and 1.35. howItsDone now names Lumen Gentium 8, which quotes City of God 18.51 on the Church pressing forward 'like a pilgrim'; confirm. Pronunciation of civitas changed to Church Latin (CHEE-), matching the other Latin on this path.
